Volume I gives a detailed account of this man, who led the Zanj revolt with remarkable courage and organizational skill. These qualities made the revolt one of the major uprisings in the history of social struggle, despite mistakes that could hardly have been avoided under the historical conditions of the time.↩︎

The Zanj revolt was purely a class revolt, not a racial struggle between Black and white people. This is clear from its social and economic conditions, from the fact that its leadership was white—its first leader, ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad, and his associates ʿAlī ibn Abān, Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad, and Muḥammad ibn Salm—and from the fact that large groups of Bedouin Arabs and non-Zanj peasants gave valuable support by supplying its armies. See ʿAlī, p. 114; al-Ṭabarī, vol. 8, pp. 91, 95; and ʿAbd al-Fattāḥ ʿUlyān, Qarāmiṭat al-ʿIrāq, p. 24, citing Nöldeke, Sketches from Eastern History, pp. 152–153.↩︎

The name “Qarmatians” most likely comes from the man who first organized the movement and spread it in the region of Kufa, from which it later expanded into the areas where history records its presence. His name was Ḥamdān Qarmaṭ. He was a poor agricultural laborer from a village near Kufa. Around 264 AH/877 CE he came into contact with an Ismaʿili missionary known as al-Ḥusayn al-Ahwāzī, who brought him into the movement and entrusted him with spreading its message and organizing its followers in that area. The Qarmatians themselves, however, did not call their community by the name by which history came to know them. They called themselves “the believers made victorious by God, the supporters of His religion, and the reformers of the earth.” See ʿUlyān, al-Qarāmiṭa fī al-ʿIrāq, pp. 30, 35, 76.↩︎

al-Baghdādī says of the people from the tribes of southern Iraq and the Syrian desert who answered the Qarmatian call that they were proverbial for their poverty and hunger (al-Farq bayna al-Firaq, p. 142). Abū al-Faḍl, al-Ishāra fī Maḥāsin al-Tijāra, Cairo, 1318 AH, p. 43, describes the craftsmen and ordinary people in the towns who joined the movement as the poorest among the free population.↩︎

The Nabataeans were “a non-Arab people who lived between the two Iraqs. They were called Nabataeans because they drew out what the land produced; the word later came to be used for mixed groups of people and for the common population” (al-Munjid, entry “Nabaṭ”). Dr. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Dūrī says that the term refers to the ancient peasants of Iraq who spoke Aramaic. After the Persians weakened them, they were absorbed among the Persians and came to identify with them. They later converted to Islam and spoke a rough form of Arabic, but kept many of their pre-Islamic traditions. Some Bedouins also settled among them, and the whole population came to be known as people of the Sawād. See al-Dūrī, Tārīkh al-ʿIrāq al-Iqtiṣādī fī al-Qarn al-Rābiʿ al-Hijrī, Baghdad, 1948, p. 26.↩︎

One example is the revolt of Abū Ḥarb al-Mubarqaʿ al-Yamānī during the caliphate of al-Muʿtaṣim ibn al-Rashīd. Abū Ḥarb appeared in the mountains of Jordan and declared rebellion against the state, wearing a veil over his face during the day to conceal his identity. Many peasants in the region joined him. The state was unable to crush his movement until the planting season, when his peasant followers became occupied with working the land. Other examples include the revolt of the Alid al-Ḥasan ibn Zayd and his establishment of an Alid state in Ṭabaristān; the rise of the Ṣaffārid state in Ṭabaristān, 254–290 AH; and Aḥmad ibn Ṭūlūn’s establishment of an independent state in Egypt. See ʿUlyān, Qarāmiṭat al-ʿIrāq, pp. 125, 127.↩︎

When the Abbasid caliph al-Muʿtazz ibn al-Mutawakkil (252–255 AH/866–868 CE) could no longer tolerate the pressure placed on him by the Turkish troops and their demands, he tried to counter them by calling on the Maghribi troops—that is, the Arab soldiers in the Abbasid army. But al-Muʿtazz was unable to pay the soldiers’ wages, so the Turkish and Arab troops ended up united against the caliph himself and together took part in killing him. See Ibn al-Wardī, Tārīkh, p. 332. In other words, the Arab soldiers’ hostility toward the politically dominant Turks did not prevent them from joining their “class comrades,” the Turkish soldiers, when their shared material interests brought them together—even though the caliph they killed was himself an Arab.↩︎

One of the many ways ordinary people engaged in social struggle at the time can be seen in the following incident. After the killing of al-Muʿtazz ibn al-Mutawakkil, the Turks installed Muḥammad ibn al-Wāthiq as caliph and gave him the title al-Muhtadī (255–256 AH/868–869 CE). But al-Muhtadī disappointed them. He tried to reduce extravagance, improve the machinery of government, and improve the condition of those suffering injustice. This angered the Turks who had put him in power, and they began plotting to remove him or kill him, as they had done before. The “common people” sensed the beginnings of the plot and took a stand in defense of the caliph. They prepared leaflets and scattered them in the streets and mosques. The leaflets read: “Muslims! Pray to God for your just caliph, that God may give him victory over his enemy, protect him from his oppressor, and complete His blessing upon him and upon this community by preserving his life. The Turks have forced him to abdicate.” See al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Umam, vol. 7, pp. 571–572.↩︎
The Sawād of Kufa means its villages and countryside.↩︎

“The sciences of the ancients” was a term used by medieval Arab scholars, philosophers, and historians of philosophy for the ancient natural and philosophical sciences that were translated into Arabic and then became part of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage. The term refers above all to the sciences of ancient Greece, but also to Persian, Indian, and other ancient sources that contributed to Arab culture in the Abbasid period. We prefer this older term to the modern expression “foreign sciences” when speaking of medieval Arab culture. “The sciences of the ancients” reflects a scientific view of civilization as a historical succession shared among peoples, nations, and regions, without restricting it to one people or one geographical area. “Foreign sciences,” by contrast, implies an opposite and unscientific view of civilization. No science is “foreign” in relation to any people on earth.↩︎

We find an example of this contradiction in Goldziher. On the one hand, he looks for the source of Muslim asceticism in what he calls “the Indian ideal of life” (Introduction to Islamic Theology and Law, p. 159). On the other hand, he says that “the tendency toward asceticism was connected with revolt against the existing authority,” and that many Muslims “withdrew into seclusion and asceticism as a protest against the government and social order they rejected” (ibid., p. 147). We find similar examples among modern researchers such as Muḥammad ʿAlī Abū Rayyān, Tārīkh al-Fikr al-Falsafī fī al-Islām, pp. 258, 270, and Kāmil Muṣṭafā al-Shaybī, al-Ṣila bayna al-Taṣawwuf wa-l-Tashayyuʿ, pp. 242, 243, 247.
